stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Companies that have tried a four-day week without cutting pay, the author reports, have mostly kept it. Employees, given a day back, cut the meetings and idle hours that had filled the fifth, and output in trials across several countries held steady while sick days fell and resignations dropped by more than a third. The author argues that the five-day week was never a law of nature; it was a compromise struck a century ago for factory labor, and knowledge work has simply inherited it. A schedule that produces the same work with less exhaustion is not a perk, the text concludes. It is the correction of a mistake.
stimulus.text_b: The four-day trials are encouraging, this author allows, but they share a flaw: the companies that volunteer for them are the ones most likely to succeed. They are small, office-based, and already flexible. A hospital, a school, or a restaurant cannot compress a week; it can only hire more people, which the trials' accounting never includes. Even in offices, the author notes, the gains came partly from cutting work that was wasteful in the first place, which a firm could do on any schedule. The text does not oppose shorter weeks. It warns that a result from firms that chose to be studied cannot be assumed to hold for firms that did not.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Banning thin plastic grocery bags, the author argues, is one of the rare environmental policies that costs almost nothing and works. Within a year of one city's ban, the number of plastic bags found in storm drains and along the shoreline fell by roughly half, and shoppers adapted within weeks, as they had been told they would not. The bag itself was never essential; it was a convenience that had become a habit, and habits can be changed by a small, well-timed push. The author sees the ban as a model: pick the waste that is most visible, most avoidable, and least missed.
stimulus.text_b: The bans do reduce litter, this author agrees, but their effect on the environment as a whole is less clear. When thin bags disappear, shoppers buy thicker plastic bags for trash cans and pet waste, and many of the reusable bags handed out in their place are made of materials that require dozens of uses before they outperform the bag they replaced. Studies in several cities find total plastic consumption falling by far less than the bag count suggests. The author does not call for repealing the bans. The point is that a visible result is not the same as a large one, and that policy should be judged by the second.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Raising the minimum age for social media accounts to sixteen, the author argues, is the least a society can do for its adolescents. The years between twelve and fifteen are when self-image is most fragile, and platforms built to maximize attention have learned to exploit that fragility with comparison, notification, and the quiet arithmetic of likes. Surveys of teenagers themselves find that most wish they used the apps less and cannot manage to. An age limit does not solve everything. It gives families a rule to point to, and it gives the youngest users three more years before the pressure begins.
stimulus.text_b: The evidence linking social media to adolescent distress, this author notes, is weaker and more mixed than headlines suggest, and age limits carry costs that advocates rarely weigh. For isolated teenagers, including those in rural areas or with uncommon interests, the apps are where they find the only people who understand them. A ban would push younger users onto platforms with no safety features at all, since enforcement by birthdate is trivially evaded. The author favors stricter design rules, such as limits on notifications and infinite scrolling, that would apply to every user. Fix the product, the text argues, rather than fencing off the people.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Requiring students to memorize poems, the author argues, is not an antique practice but a gift. A poem carried in memory is available anywhere: on a bus, in a hospital waiting room, at a graveside. Students who learn lines by heart come to feel the rhythm of the language from the inside, in a way that reading silently never provides, and they acquire a store of phrases that will shape how they write and speak for the rest of their lives. The objection that memorization is mere rote misses the point. One does not memorize a poem instead of understanding it. One memorizes it in order to understand it slowly, over years.
stimulus.text_b: Memorization has its pleasures, this author grants, but classroom time is scarce and should go where it does the most good. An hour spent drilling lines is an hour not spent discussing what a poem means, comparing it with another, or writing in response to it. The students who thrive at recitation are often those who already love the material; for the rest, the assignment confirms a suspicion that poetry is a performance of obedience. If the goal is a lifelong relationship with poems, the author suggests, it is better served by teaching students how to find and read new ones than by fixing a few old ones in their heads.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Students who take notes by hand, the author reports, consistently remember more of a lecture than those who type. Because writing is slower, they cannot transcribe, so they must decide what matters and put it in their own words, and that act of compression is itself a form of learning. Typists, by contrast, tend to produce near-verbatim records that they never fully process. In several experiments, the handwriting advantage held even when typists were explicitly warned not to transcribe. The author concludes that the pen's limitations are a feature, and recommends that lecture halls discourage laptops.
stimulus.text_b: The author accepts the finding that handwriting aids memory in the lecture hall but questions the recommendation that follows. The experiments measured recall of a single lecture within a week. They did not measure what students did afterward with their notes, and typed notes are far easier to search, reorganize, and share when preparing for an exam weeks later. Nor did the studies include students with disabilities, for whom a keyboard may be the only practical option. Rather than banning laptops, the author suggests teaching students to type the way good note-takers write: selectively, in their own words, and with the lecture rather than the screen as the focus.

choices.text: individual productivity did not decline when employees began working from home
choices.rationale: Correct. Text 1 reports steady or rising productivity, and Text 2 says 'individual output may hold up.'

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Supporters of remote work point to a decade of surveys in which employees report doing more in fewer hours when they work from home. The savings are not mysterious: no commute, fewer interruptions, and the freedom to schedule deep work when one's attention is sharpest. Companies that measured output rather than hours, the author notes, found that productivity held steady or rose when offices closed, while turnover fell. The office, on this view, was never where the work got done; it was where the work got watched. A firm that insists on attendance is paying for supervision it does not need and losing workers who can find flexibility elsewhere.
stimulus.text_b: The productivity gains reported by remote workers are real but misleading, this author argues, because they measure the wrong period. In the first year of working from home, employees drew on relationships and shared knowledge built over years in the office. The question is what happens when that stock runs down. Studies tracking new hires who never met their colleagues in person find slower skill growth and weaker ties to the people who could help them. Individual output may hold up; the collective capacity to train, mentor, and improvise together erodes quietly. The office, the author concludes, was less a place of supervision than a place of apprenticeship.

stimulus.title: Paired passages
stimulus.text: Spending billions to send people to other worlds while problems remain unsolved at home, the author argues, reflects misplaced priorities. The money devoted to a single crewed mission could fund clean water for millions or research into diseases that kill every year. Robots, moreover, can collect most of the scientific data humans could, at a fraction of the cost and risk. The romance of exploration is real, but romance is a poor basis for budgets. A government's first obligation is to the people who already live on the planet it governs, and every launch should be weighed against what the same money could do for them.
stimulus.text_b: The author does not dispute that needs on Earth are urgent, but argues that framing the choice as exploration versus welfare is false. Space budgets are a small fraction of national spending, far smaller than most people guess, and cutting them would not transfer the savings to clean water; it would simply reduce them. Meanwhile, the engineering required to keep humans alive in hostile environments has produced water purification, medical monitoring, and weather forecasting that serve people who will never leave Earth. The question, the text suggests, is not whether to look up or down, but whether we can do both well.
